video_title: How to Get Out of a Bubble Without Selling Too Early: Jeff deGraaf Explains
gist: RenMac's Jeff deGraaf argues US real yields near 2.65% (above Bagehot's 2% threshold) make bonds a real alternative to an S&P whose FCF yield has fallen to the same level, tightening conditions that favor defensives, value and quality while widening credit spreads. He explains RenMac's bubble indicator (index doubling within two years from a high) and 'shoot them in the back' exit, which caught the June semiconductor peak, and calls private credit 'stably deteriorating'.

themes.theme: Real yields above 2%: bonds are back as an alternative

insights.claim: Walter Bagehot's 1873 'John Bull can't stand 2%' proverb describes how sub-2% returns under hard money pushed investors out the risk curve into Central/South American railroad bonds that defaulted within four or five years at 9-12% yields.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Sub-2% real yields historically breed reach-for-yield speculation that ends in defaults; watch the regime, not just the asset.
insights.quote: John Bull can stand many things but John Bull can't stand 2%

insights.claim: The post-GFC TINA era through roughly 2022, created by Fed QE suppressing rates, pushed investors into equities and speculative vehicles like SPACs, analogous to the 1873 Honduran railroad bonds.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Speculation built under zero real rates is vulnerable now that the rate regime has flipped.

insights.claim: US real yields (nominal minus inflation expectations) are in the high 2s, about 2.65% at recording versus 2.90% when RenMac wrote the piece, above the 2% threshold that makes bonds competitive.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Real yields above 2% are a regime change that should gradually pull allocations away from equities.
insights.quote: that real rate is in the high twos. I think it's 2.65 today when we wrote the piece it was 2.90

insights.claim: With ~5% nominal and ~2.6% real yields, a 65/35 stock/bond portfolio can approach a 7% target return that previously required something like an 80/15 equity-heavy allocation, with much less volatility.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Rebalance toward bonds: you can hit return targets with lower volatility now.

insights.claim: deGraaf expects the shift out of equities into bonds to be gradual rather than a 'thunderclap', happening as investors grow frustrated with equity losses, possibly starting with the unwind in AI semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Expect slow, persistent rotation flows into fixed income rather than a single crash.
insights.quote: I don't think it really ends up being, you know, kind of a thunderclap. I think it ends up being kind of this gradual move

insights.claim: Real yields above 2% have not historically meant equities underperform; the benefit is that a balanced portfolio can add value by lowering volatility.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Higher real yields argue for diversification, not necessarily for shorting stocks.

insights.claim: The S&P 500's free-cash-flow-to-enterprise-value yield was about 4.5% when QE/TINA began but is now roughly 2-2.75%, in line with TIPS real yields, so stocks offer the same real yield with far more volatility.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Equity risk premium versus real bonds is essentially gone; bonds win on risk-adjusted terms.
insights.quote: Today, it's right in line with what you're getting on these real yields

insights.claim: Higher term premium may reflect the Treasury competing with corporate issuers like Google and Meta for capital (crowding out) and distrust of the fiscal situation and expected supply.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler debt issuance is a factor in rising long-end yields; watch issuance calendars.
insights.quote: the Treasury is now competing with Google, right, who's issuing debt and Meta who's issuing debt

insights.claim: RenMac's five-year-return-by-gap-quintile study back to 1953 places the current equity-versus-bond valuation gap in the second-worst quintile, where stocks beat bonds only 63% of the time with muted returns.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Forward five-year equity returns versus bonds look below average from here.

insights.claim: Real yields hitting 2% is not itself the allocation trigger: RenMac found it statistically better to let rising yields run and shift into bonds only once yields roll over with technical confirmation.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Use trend confirmation (yields peaking) to time a bond allocation rather than a fixed level.
insights.quote: you're better just letting it go. So two on its way to three or three on its way to four

insights.claim: Holding real-yielding bonds as ballast lets a portfolio rebalance in a 15-20% S&P correction (e.g., from 65/35 drifting to 50/50), selling bonds at a gain to buy cheaper stocks, which many equity-heavy portfolios cannot currently do.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Build dry powder in bonds now so you can buy a correction.
insights.quote: There's no there's no cushion, right? There's no there's nothing to reallocate.

insights.claim: The bond market is the final adjudicator of fiscal plans, echoing Bill Clinton's complaint about being beholden to bond traders, and term premium is rising globally after the election.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Post-election fiscal proposals will be judged by long-end yields; watch term premium globally.
insights.quote: what do you mean I'm um you know, my economic plans are beholden to a bunch of bond traders

themes.theme: Tightening conditions: credit spreads and sector rotation

insights.claim: Higher real rates are a tightening of financial conditions that typically filters next into wider corporate spreads, already visible in CCCs.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Expect credit to underperform as real rates stay high; watch spreads as the transmission channel.

insights.claim: BB spreads are about 196 bp, right at RenMac's 200 bp threshold that signals deteriorating credit.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: A break above 200 bp in BB spreads would be a credit-deterioration trigger.
insights.quote: We look for basically a 200 basis point spread as kind of a hey things are deteriorating. We're at about 196 here.

insights.claim: CCC spreads are around 1,200 bp but the median is far lower, meaning about four or five issuers account for most of the stress, so CCC deterioration is still narrow, not broad-based.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Index-level CCC spread overstates breadth of stress; track the median and breadth.

insights.claim: About 7% of CCC names trade below 80% of par, the dividing line between good and shaky credit, and that share is expanding.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Rising share of bonds below 80 of par is the breadth signal for a credit cycle turn.

insights.claim: Cable names and hyperscalers are among the cohort driving CCC/elevated spreads, and a third of hyperscalers' bonds trade at their widest spreads of the last two years.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Credit is pricing AI-capex risk at hyperscalers even while equity holders focus on growth.
insights.quote: a third of the um hyperscalers are trading at um at their widest of the last two years

insights.claim: RenMac defines cyclicality by correlation to forward GDP: tech, discretionary and industrials are most cyclical; healthcare, staples and utilities least, and no sector is negatively correlated to GDP.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Higher real yields favor healthcare, staples and utilities over tech, discretionary and industrials.

insights.claim: Higher real yields tilt styles toward quality and value, and value versus growth has recently had a big relative-performance breakout.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Lean into quality and value factors while real yields stay above 2%.
insights.quote: We've had a big breakout in the value versus versus growth relative performance here recently.

insights.claim: The market is doing some of the Fed's tightening for it amid expectations for rate hikes under Chair Powell.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Market-driven tightening reduces the need for hikes but still pressures cyclicals and credit.

themes.theme: Bubble signal and 'shoot them in the back'

insights.claim: RenMac's bubble indicator fires when an index doubles within two years measured from an all-time high (not a low); for commodities and single stocks the window is shortened to six months. It has triggered in the Hang Seng, biotech, China in 2008 and recently semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: A systematic, rules-based bubble definition you can replicate on any index.
insights.quote: The bubble indicator is simply a doubling of an index.

insights.claim: After a bubble signal, the asset is higher three months later about 80% of the time, roughly 50/50 at six months, and tends to round-trip back to the signal level, with V-tops becoming far more likely.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Stay long ~3 months after a bubble trigger, then get defensive; expect full retracement to the trigger price.
insights.quote: The the first 3 months, 80% of the time it's going to be higher. Um 6 months more 50/50

insights.claim: The 'shoot them in the back' strategy rides a bubble and sells on the first crack on the way down rather than trying to top-tick on the way up, which maximizes terminal wealth and avoids FOMO re-entry like Isaac Newton's.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Trailing exits beat pre-emptive selling in bubbles.
insights.quote: your terminal wealth is going to be better by shooting it in the back than believing that you can pick the top on the way up

insights.claim: Isaac Newton quintupled his South Sea Company money by February 1720, sold, watched it triple, then reinvested near the top including proceeds from his Bank of England shares, and still held much of it at his death.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Even brilliant investors fall to bubble FOMO; have rules before the mania.

insights.claim: The semiconductor bubble signal fired in late April; deGraaf told CNBC to own it for three months, and semis peaked June 22, about two months later.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: The bubble framework called the semis top within its window.

insights.claim: In bubbles participants become 'one-dimensional' (in semis: AI, memory, 85% gross margins, three years of capacity), so the contrarian move is to ask what can go wrong; during the tariff tantrum he asked what can go right instead.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: When narrative concentrates on one factor, look for the overlooked risk (credit, regulation).
insights.quote: we're always trying to pay attention to when the market becomes very singularly focused and very one-dimensional because that's when there's a lot of opportunities

insights.claim: Using point-in-time data, the SOX was already down 40% in 2000 before the first downward earnings-estimate revision, so waiting for revisions is a poor exit signal.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Don't wait for analyst cuts to exit semis; price leads revisions.
insights.quote: the socks was down 40% by the time you had your first earnings estimate revision downward

insights.claim: Prediction-market odds shifting toward a blue wave (Republicans holding the Senate falling from ~60% to ~40%; blue wave in both houses at 70%) signaled regulatory risk for the AI/semis trade that investors focused on data-center build-out ignored.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Regulatory regime risk after the election is a new headwind for AI names.

insights.claim: deGraaf thinks the semiconductor unwind is roughly midway, will be more time than price, still awaits downward revisions and a disgust phase (ETF outflows, put-heavy options), and historically takes about 13 months, making a washout a 2027 rather than 2026 event.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Don't bottom-fish semis yet; look for washout signals around mid-2027.
insights.quote: I think it's fair to say it's a 2027 event, not a 2026 event

insights.claim: Small modular reactors, uranium and quantum computing stocks all triggered bubble signals about a year ago, and the 18-month forward return for bubble-signal names is poor on average.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Avoid chasing hot thematic stocks after a bubble trigger; consider hedging them.
insights.quote: The 18 month return tends to be pretty poor on average for those names.

insights.claim: Buying puts on bubble names is too expensive because volatility is so high; selling calls to build a synthetic short is the preferred hedge, with the risk that one in eight keeps steamrolling higher.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Monetize elevated vol by selling calls on bubble names rather than buying puts.

insights.claim: Gold's bubble signal fired last October, it rose three months, cracked in January, has fully retraced to the signal level amid apathy and outflows, and could become interesting if it breaks out.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Gold has 'done the cleanse'; watch for a breakout as a fresh long setup.
insights.quote: If we can break gold out, like we've we've kind of done the cleanse.

themes.theme: Regime analysis, market cycle clock and position sizing

insights.claim: RenMac's approach separates conditional factors/regime analysis (how much to bet: the fuel) from technical triggers (when to act: the spark).
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Size by regime, time by trend.
insights.quote: the conditions are how much fuel's in the tank, right? And then the technicals are where is the spark coming in

insights.claim: RenMac's market cycle clock (proprietary inflation vs growth, back to the mid-1940s) places the US in the top third for inflation and roughly the 60-65th percentile for growth, the zone with the worst historical S&P annualized return, only about +40 bp.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Macro regime argues against leaning into equities; tighten stops.
insights.quote: the historical annualized return for the S&P in this zone is the worst of of any

insights.claim: The current market cycle clock zone is consistent with higher back-end rates, a flattening curve and higher real rates, and historically favors energy and healthcare while materials and discretionary lag.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Overweight energy and healthcare, underweight materials and discretionary.
insights.quote: What's interesting is also it's the best zone for energy.

insights.claim: Acting on the market cycle clock alone would have meant selling equities around February, far too early, which is why RenMac waits for technical confirmation.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Macro regime signals are early; pair with trend.

insights.claim: RenMac sizes positions with the Kelly criterion, signal-to-noise ratios and volatility adjustment to equalize risk across the book, something most non-quant investors overlook.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Volatility-adjusting position sizes is a cheap edge for discretionary investors.

insights.claim: deGraaf argues conviction and stubbornness differ only by outcome, so investors must be pragmatic and use technicals to stress-test ideas daily; across hundreds of studies, 'up is good, down is bad'.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Avoid buying falling stocks or selling rising ones; follow trend.
insights.quote: what's the difference between conviction and stubbornness, right? It's outcome.

insights.claim: Private credit grew out of post-GFC Dodd-Frank limits on bank lending, effectively shadow banking now dominated by private equity firms whose credit arms are often bigger than their PE arms.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Private credit is the system's new levered lender and the likely locus of the next credit stress.

insights.claim: Rapid growth in private credit led to lowered standards, covenant-lite terms, PIK and 'extend and pretend', with blowups like First Brands where claimed overcollateralization didn't exist.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Opacity plus fast growth is a classic setup for credit losses.
insights.quote: Whenever I see growth in financials for an extended period of time, anything financial, you have to worry about

insights.claim: Many private credit loans are floating rate and were struck when real rates were near zero, so higher real rates are increasingly burdensome for borrowers.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Higher-for-longer real rates directly erode private credit borrower coverage.

insights.claim: Redemption gates (typically ~5%) are being hit as investors request 7-12%, turning a liquidity problem into what can become a solvency problem if prolonged.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Track gate activations and redemption requests as the key private credit stress gauge.
insights.quote: I don't have a solvency problem. I have a liquidity

insights.claim: BDCs and the private equity ETF PSP have been under pressure, with markets confirming RenMac's April view that a slow credit cycle has become a real but non-systemic turn, 'stably deteriorating'.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Short/avoid BDCs and listed PE as the credit turn proceeds.
insights.quote: right now it seems to be stably deteriorating is the way I would uh I would put it

insights.claim: deGraaf sees the business cycle trying to turn, slowed mainly because AI spending has kept it going.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: If AI capex slows, the cycle turn could accelerate.

insights.claim: A private credit refinancing wall hits mostly in 2029, when loans struck at 3-5% may reset near 10%, and software-heavy credit faces existential AI disruption (the 'SaaS apocalypse').
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Software-backed loans are the most vulnerable segment; watch the 2029 maturity wall.
insights.quote: do you do you still need to have this software company when, you know, you could cloud code it in in afternoon maybe?

insights.claim: Bitcoin and crypto diverged positively after Treasury Secretary Bessen (Bessent) floated buying back-end off-the-run securities; gold gave back its rally but crypto held, an early potentially bullish trend change awaiting follow-through.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Watch crypto for confirmation of a new uptrend.

insights.claim: November is historically the best month, positive about 77% of the time with about a 260 bp average return, roughly 3x a normal month, creating tactical upside even though structural conditions are weak.
insights.speaker: Jeff deGraaf
insights.so_what: Trade year-end seasonality tactically but sell into resistance given weak structural backdrop.
insights.quote: about a 77% uh chance historically of probable positive returns with about a 260 basis point return
